title: Fix data integrity before any spend, creative or budget call
hypothesis: If we fix tracking, exclusions and COGS tagging before reading performance, then later spend and creative decisions stop compounding on false signals.

signal.check: No documented check this quarter of 7-day-click reporting, existing-customer exclusions, COGS tagging and CAPI firing before the last budget change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a precondition for every other number, not a lift on its own

risk.note: A checklist review of existing setup; no live change to the store or ads.

prerequisites: Access to ad account reporting settings and order-level data
steps: Check whether reported ROAS uses 1-day view or 7-day click as the headline number.
Confirm existing customers are excluded from cold prospecting campaigns.
Confirm COGS is tagged per SKU, not a flat assumed margin.
Confirm new vs returning customer revenue is split with order counts.
Confirm CAPI or server-side tracking is firing on purchase events.
Fix any gap found, then re-read the last month's numbers before deciding anything else.

test.method: Run the 9-point data integrity checklist once, then monthly.
test.measure: count of integrity issues found and fixed
test.read_point: Before the next spend or budget decision

title: Split every revenue ratio into new-customer and returning-customer lines
hypothesis: If we compute every ratio on net revenue split by new vs returning customer, then paid media stops getting credit for revenue that product and repeat behaviour actually produced.

signal.check: Reports show one blended revenue and CAC number with no new-customer column.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reporting fix, not a revenue lift

risk.note: A reporting change; does not touch live campaigns.

prerequisites: Order data with a first-order date per customer
steps: Tag every order as new or returning from the customer's first-order date.
Rebuild net revenue as gross revenue minus refunds, discounts and shipping allowances.
Report new-customer and returning-customer revenue and order counts as separate lines every month.
Stop crediting paid media with returning-customer revenue.

test.method: Compare the new blended-vs-split view for the last 6 months.
test.measure: gap between blended and new-customer revenue trend
test.read_point: Once, then monthly going forward

title: Track AMER for media spend decisions, not just blended MER
hypothesis: If we hold the media buyer to new-customer revenue over spend (AMER) instead of blended MER, then we stop scaling spend on a metric that returning customers can inflate while acquisition quietly worsens.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with almost no returning revenue, where MER and AMER already track closely

signal.check: MER is flat or rising while new-customer revenue and order count are falling.

expected_effect.size: example given: MER 4x to 5x while AMER fell 2.0x to 1.8x to 1.6x in one case

risk.note: A metric change; blocks a spend increase rather than making one.

prerequisites: New vs returning revenue split in place
steps: Compute AMER = new-customer net revenue / ad spend, monthly.
Compute MER = total net revenue / ad spend, monthly.
Plot both trends together every month.
If MER rises while AMER falls, block any spend increase until the gap is explained.

test.method: Track AMER and MER side by side.
test.read_point: Monthly, before any scale decision

title: Use true gross margin, never product margin, for any spend decision
hypothesis: If we subtract shipping out, pick and pack, transaction fees and refund allowance from product margin, then break-even ROAS and discount limits are calculated from the real number, not an inflated one.

signal.check: Marketing decisions use a quoted product margin (price minus unit cost) with no delivery costs subtracted.

expected_effect.size: one example moved from 70% product margin to 24% true gross margin

risk.note: A recalculation; no live change until a decision is made on the corrected number.

prerequisites: Per-SKU cost of delivery data (freight in, shipping out, pick and pack, transaction fees)
steps: List every cost line beyond unit cost: freight in, shipping out, pick and pack, transaction fees, sales tax flow-through, landed freight, refund allowance.
Subtract all of them from price per SKU to get true gross margin.
Recompute for any planned discount depth as well as full price.
Replace the quoted product margin with true gross margin in every budget and break-even model.

test.method: Recompute true gross margin per SKU once, then every quarter or after a cost change.
test.measure: gap between quoted margin and true gross margin
test.read_point: Before any marketing budget or promotion is modelled

title: Tag COGS per SKU so gross margin updates live during a discount
hypothesis: If COGS is tagged per SKU instead of assumed as a flat margin, then gross margin during a discount is calculated correctly instead of hidden.

signal.check: A storewide discount is being planned and the margin model still uses one flat assumed margin percent.

expected_effect.size: example: a 20% storewide discount on a 50% GM product drops true margin to 37.5%, a 30% relative drop

risk.note: A data setup task.

prerequisites: Product cost fields in the store or ERP system
steps: Add a COGS field to every active SKU.
Recompute margin live as price and discount change, not from a fixed percent.
Require this before modelling any promotion.
Flag any SKU missing a COGS field before it goes on promotion.

test.method: Compare margin at 0%, 10% and 20% discount using live COGS.
test.measure: true gross margin at each discount depth
test.read_point: Before any promotion is approved

title: Judge CAC against first-purchase gross profit, not on its own
hypothesis: If we compute CAC from order data and pair it with first-purchase gross profit on new customers, then we can tell whether the brand depends on repeat purchase to break even, instead of judging CAC in isolation.

signal.check: CAC is reported without a matching first-purchase gross profit or GP:CAC ratio.

expected_effect.size: a disclosed example fell from about 2x to 1.03x over 6 quarters as volume scaled

risk.note: A calculation change; no live spend change on its own.

prerequisites: New-customer order data
True gross margin per SKU
steps: Compute CAC = total ad spend across all platforms (including creator and affiliate cost) / new customers from order data.
Compute first-purchase GP per new customer = new-customer AOV x true gross margin % on the new-customer product mix.
Compute first-purchase GP:CAC monthly.
If below 1.0, note that the brand depends on repeat purchase to break even and check cohort data next.

test.method: Track first-purchase GP:CAC monthly.
test.read_point: Monthly, before any spend increase

title: Recompute break-even ROAS and CAC before any promotion
hypothesis: If we calculate break-even ROAS as 1 divided by true gross margin percent at each planned discount depth, then we know before launch which discount depths are unreachable at a profit.

signal.check: A promotion or sale is being planned without a recalculated break-even ROAS at that discount depth.

expected_effect.size: rises linearly with discount depth; the ROAS needed to hold a fixed contribution target rises faster than linearly

risk.note: A formula check before a promotion runs.

prerequisites: True gross margin per SKU
steps: Compute break-even ROAS = 1 / true gross margin % for the SKU or mix at full price.
Recompute at each planned discount depth with all cost lines included.
Compute break-even CAC = gross margin dollars per order at that discount depth.
Compare the achievable ROAS to the break-even ROAS before approving the promotion depth.

test.method: Model break-even ROAS at 0, 10, 20 and 30% off before the sale.
test.read_point: Before any sale or promotion is set

title: Set the LTGP:CAC window to your own repurchase category, not a generic lifetime
hypothesis: If we measure LTGP:CAC in a fixed window sized to the category's repurchase frequency instead of an unbounded lifetime, then the ratio is comparable across time and can guide a scale, hold or stop decision.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with fewer than 30 days of cohort history; use first-purchase GP:CAC instead until cohorts mature

signal.check: LTGP:CAC is quoted as a lifetime number with no stated window, or the window does not match the category's repeat cycle.

expected_effect.size: bands cited: below 1.0 = spiral risk, 1 to 2 = tight, 2 to 3 = scale, above 3 = may be underinvesting (cash exception applies)

risk.note: A measurement change; the scale/hold/stop decision it feeds is where the real risk sits.

prerequisites: Cohort gross profit data at 30, 90, 180 or 365 days
steps: Pick the window by category: near first-purchase only for furniture and one-off considered purchases; 180 to 365 days for subscription and consumables.
Compute LTGP = revenue minus COGS minus cost of delivery over that window, per acquisition cohort.
Divide by CAC for that cohort to get LTGP:CAC.
Flag any window that extends past the oldest real cohort as modelled, not measured.
Compare against the bands and decide: stop scaling, hold, scale in steps, or scale harder unless cash-constrained.

test.method: Recompute LTGP:CAC monthly per cohort window.
test.read_point: Monthly, before any spend change

title: Target near-breakeven first-purchase profit unless repeat purchase is proven
hypothesis: If we size CAC targets from the brand's own 12-month lifetime gross profit data and aim for near-breakeven on the first order unless repeat is proven, then spend does not quietly depend on repeat purchase that has not been shown to happen.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with 12+ months of cohort data proving strong repeat, which can justify a small planned first-order loss

signal.check: First-order economics are unprofitable and no 12-month cohort data has been used to justify the planned loss.

expected_effect.size: example: $60 CAC, $40 first-order profit sized against about $400 of proven 12-month backend profit

risk.note: Wrong sizing can fund unprofitable acquisition for months before cohorts mature enough to catch it.

prerequisites: 12 months of purchase history for at least one prior cohort
steps: Pull customers who bought 12 or more months ago.
Sum their gross profit over the following 12 months.
Use that figure to size how much first-order loss the brand can afford, if any.
For one-off products, target first-order profit; only allow a small first-order loss where repeat is proven.

test.method: Recompute the allowable first-order loss whenever a new 12-month cohort completes.
test.read_point: Quarterly, as each cohort crosses 12 months

title: Gate any spend increase on payback months, recomputed at current CPM trend
hypothesis: If we recompute payback months (time until cumulative cohort gross profit exceeds CAC) after every planned spend increase, then rising CPMs are caught before they quietly lengthen payback past the brand's own gate.

signal.check: A spend increase is planned without a recomputed payback estimate at the new CPM trend.

expected_effect.size: gates vary by brand; treat under 4 months as strong, 6 as workable, 12+ as weak for most stores, subject to the brand's own cash position

risk.note: A calculation gate before a spend decision.

prerequisites: Cohort gross profit curve
steps: Compute payback months as months until cumulative cohort gross profit per customer exceeds CAC.
Recompute at the current CPM trend before approving a spend increase.
Compare against the brand's own gate, not a competitor's.
Recheck monthly since rising CPMs lengthen payback even when trailing CAC:LTV looks fine.

test.method: Recompute payback before and after each planned spend step.
test.read_point: Before every spend increase, then monthly

title: Diagnose a missed profit target by walking up the P&L waterfall
hypothesis: If we build the full waterfall (net revenue, cost of delivery, gross margin, marketing, contribution margin, opex, EBITDA, interest, net profit) and diagnose a miss by walking up from the affected line, then the fix targets the actual broken line instead of a guess.

signal.check: A profit or EBITDA miss is being discussed without a line-by-line waterfall to show which stage broke.

expected_effect.size: diagnostic only; no stated lift

risk.note: A reporting build; the fix it points to carries the real risk.

prerequisites: Monthly revenue, cost of delivery, marketing spend and opex by line
steps: Build the waterfall: net revenue, minus cost of delivery = true gross margin, minus all marketing = contribution margin, minus opex = EBITDA, minus interest = net profit.
Keep fulfilment staff and transaction fees out of opex; keep interest below EBITDA.
When a target is missed, check gross margin first (cost of delivery or revenue), then contribution margin (marketing or cost of delivery), then EBITDA (opex).
Name the exact line that broke before proposing a fix.

test.method: Rebuild the waterfall every month; walk it whenever a target is missed.
test.read_point: Monthly, and immediately after any missed target

title: Model ending cash separately from net income before setting a growth target
hypothesis: If we model the cash the next inventory buy needs separately from net income, then a growth target does not get set that looks profitable on paper but drains the bank account.

signal.check: A revenue growth target has been set without modelling the cash the matching inventory buy requires.

expected_effect.size: example: $2M of P&L profit with $3M of unsold inventory can be about $1M cash negative

risk.note: Missing this can force a rushed inventory-financing deal or a stockout.

prerequisites: Inventory on hand and on order
Supplier payment terms
Cash balance
steps: Model starting cash, inventory purchases (cash out when paid, by supplier terms), marketing, revenue, COGS, gross profit, opex and ending cash by month.
Compute cash conversion cycle = days inventory outstanding + days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding.
Compare net income and ending cash trends; investigate any month they diverge without a purchase order explaining it.
Size the cash a growth target needs before committing to it.

test.method: Run the cash model alongside the P&L every month.
test.measure: ending cash vs net income gap
test.read_point: Monthly, and before setting any growth target

title: Find the one binding cash lever among the 6, or move 2 to 3 together
hypothesis: If we test which of CAC, AOV, maintained markup, returning-customer rate, 30-day sell-through or opex actually binds cash, then we move that lever (or 2 to 3 together) instead of guessing which one to work.

signal.check: Cash is tight and no lever-by-lever model has been run to find which one binds.

expected_effect.size: one illustration roughly doubled ending cash by moving opex, markup and sell-through together, with no change to CAC, AOV or return rate

risk.note: A modelling exercise before any lever is pulled.

prerequisites: Cash model from procedure 4.1
steps: Run the base cash model 6 months forward at current inputs.
Re-run once per lever with a plausible change and read ending cash at day 30, 60, 90 and 180.
Rank levers by ending-cash effect and by feasibility; remember fixed opex cuts hit cash 1:1 while marketing cuts do not.
Pick 2 to 3 levers to move together and keep the base run as the comparison.
Reinvest any freed cash deliberately rather than letting it sit idle.

test.method: Compare the lever-adjusted model to the base run.
test.read_point: Before committing to a lever move, then at each checkpoint

title: Judge a lever change on a 60 to 180 day window, not day 30
hypothesis: If we wait 60 to 180 days before judging whether a cash lever change worked, then we do not kill a working change too early because day 30 looked flat.

signal.check: A cash-lever change was judged a failure inside 30 days of being made.

expected_effect.size: model stays roughly flat at day 30 and compounds through day 180

risk.note: A patience rule; if nothing has moved by day 90 to 180, treat the model or the change as wrong.

prerequisites: A dated baseline before the lever change
steps: Timestamp the change and record the baseline cash and CAC/LTGP series.
Set a 60 to 180 day read date before judging the change.
If nothing has moved by day 90 to 180, treat the change or the model as wrong and revisit.

test.method: Compare cash and unit economics at day 30, 90 and 180 after the change.
test.read_point: Day 90 and day 180 after the change

title: Route paid spend into C and D grade inventory to convert it to cash
hypothesis: If we grade inventory A to D and deliberately route some paid spend into C and D stock at breakeven or a small loss, then trapped cash converts faster even though the ROAS on that spend looks bad.
does_not_apply_when: A single-SKU brand with no aging inventory backlog

signal.check: Inventory has aged C or D grade stock and marketing is still judged only on blended ROAS.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a deliberate trade of margin for cash speed

risk.note: Coordinate finance and media; a team KPI'd only on ROAS will starve dead stock of spend.

prerequisites: Inventory graded A to D by age and sell-through
steps: Grade inventory A to D by age and sell-through.
Isolate C and D stock into its own funnel with a breakeven or small-loss target.
Get finance sign-off that this spend is exempt from the normal ROAS bar.
Do not cut marketing across the board when cash is tight from unsold inventory; use this funnel instead.

test.method: Run the C/D funnel for a fixed period and track sell-through.
test.read_point: After 30 to 60 days of the funnel running

title: Offset rising CPMs with CTR or conversion rate, not panic
hypothesis: If we diagnose whether CTR or conversion rate is the weak surface before reacting to a CPM rise, then we fix the actual gap instead of treating a normal yearly CPM increase as a crisis.

signal.check: CPMs have risen year over year and the response has been to add budget or panic rather than check CTR and conversion rate.

expected_effect.size: observed range: CPMs about 20 to 30% higher year on year in one agency's accounts

risk.note: A diagnostic step before any spend change.

prerequisites: CTR and conversion rate history
steps: Decompose CAC = CPC / conversion rate, and CPC = CTR x CPM.
Check which surface (creative CTR, or PDP/landing/checkout conversion rate) is below its own historical baseline.
Fix the weak surface rather than defaulting to 'creative problem' by habit.
Expect CPMs to be higher again next year and plan for a continuous small CTR or conversion gain to outpace it.

test.method: Track CTR and conversion rate against CPM trend monthly.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_overall vs cpm trend
test.read_point: Monthly

title: Test a higher AOV or longer subscription default to fund a higher allowable CPA
hypothesis: If we raise first-order AOV through bundles, prepaid tiers or a subscription default tested in an isolated funnel, then the brand can afford a higher CPA and win more of the auction, as long as CAC does not rise at the same rate.
does_not_apply_when: A consumable where a stockpile offer would kill reorder frequency

signal.check: First-order AOV has not been tested against a bundle, prepaid tier or subscription default in the last 2 quarters.

expected_effect.size: one disclosed example moved first-purchase AOV from $142 to $212 at a 40% take rate

risk.note: Switching a whole store's default billing cycle without a test can misfire; run it in an isolated funnel first.

prerequisites: A bundle, prepaid tier or subscription option to test
steps: Design a bundle, prepaid tier or subscription default that raises AOV without discounting.
Launch it in an isolated funnel or ad set, never storewide, first.
Track AOV and CAC together to confirm CAC did not rise at the same rate.
Roll out only after the isolated test confirms the funded CPA headroom.

test.method: A/B or isolated-funnel test of the new default against the current one.
test.measure: aov and cpa in the test funnel
test.read_point: After enough orders for a stable AOV read, typically 2 to 4 weeks

title: Shift focus from lowering CAC to making the current CAC work once it plateaus
hypothesis: If CAC-cutting has plateaued on a well-optimized account, then shift effort to retention and backend value instead of chasing further CAC reductions that are very hard to get.
does_not_apply_when: A brand whose category day-365 GP lift is near zero (furniture, homewares); CAC discipline stays primary there

signal.check: CAC has been flat despite repeated optimization attempts over 2 or more months.

expected_effect.size: unknown; retention is downstream of product, portfolio and experience, not a guaranteed lift from tactics alone

risk.note: A reallocation of effort, not a live change to ads.

prerequisites: Category-band context for expected repeat rate
steps: Confirm CAC has plateaued despite genuine optimization attempts.
Check the category band for expected day-365 gross profit lift before investing heavily in retention tactics.
If the category supports repeat, prioritize product, portfolio and backend experience work over more CAC tactics.
If the category does not support repeat, keep CAC discipline as the primary lever instead.

test.method: Track category-adjusted repeat rate after retention investment.
test.read_point: One quarter after the retention work starts

title: Watch for the death spiral: rising CAC, falling volume, spend raised to compensate
hypothesis: If we monitor CAC, new-customer volume and revenue together every month, then we catch the death spiral (CAC creeps up, spend is raised to hold revenue, CAC rises again) before it roughly doubles CAC.

signal.check: CAC is breaking upward while new-customer volume and revenue fall, and spend was raised to try to hold revenue.

expected_effect.size: the loop rarely self-corrects until CAC has roughly doubled if left unaddressed

risk.note: A monitoring rule; the response it triggers carries the real work.

prerequisites: Monthly CAC, new-customer volume and revenue series
steps: Build a monthly table of CAC, new-customer volume and new-customer revenue.
Watch for CAC rising while volume and revenue fall.
Watch for a blended P&L looking fine while the first-time-customer P&L goes negative.
Watch for reported ROAS improving while profit and revenue stay flat.
If any pattern appears, do not raise spend to hold revenue; move to the death-spiral response instead.

test.method: Review the CAC/volume/revenue table monthly.
test.measure: cpa trend vs new-customer volume trend
test.read_point: Monthly

title: Run a first-time vs returning P&L split when acquisition may be loss-making
hypothesis: If we split the P&L into first-time and returning orders with every line tagged, then we can see whether returning-customer profit is quietly subsidizing loss-making acquisition, and size that subsidy on purpose.

signal.check: The blended P&L looks healthy but new-customer volume or CAC trends raise doubt about first-time profitability.

expected_effect.size: one illustration: minus $50k first-time profit funded by plus $300k returning profit

risk.note: A reporting build; the decision it informs (fund the gap or not) carries the real risk.

prerequisites: Orders tagged first-time vs returning
Cost of delivery and marketing cost allocable by order type
steps: Tag every order and every cost line as first-time or returning.
Build a separate P&L for each.
If first-time is negative, document the funding route (verified returning-customer subsidy, capital, or debt) and set a limit on it.
Timestamp the split against the CAC and LTGP series so a structural change can be compared before and after.

test.method: Run the 2-P&L split whenever a subsidy is suspected, at minimum quarterly.
test.measure: first-time P&L result vs returning P&L result
test.read_point: Quarterly, or immediately if the death-spiral check fires

title: Cap fixed opex at what the current LTGP:CAC can carry before adding headcount
hypothesis: If we confirm the current LTGP:CAC can carry a new fixed cost before adding it, then opex does not grow faster than gross margin during a growth phase and quietly erase profit.

signal.check: Opex as a percent of revenue has risen over the last 6 months while LTGP:CAC has not improved.

expected_effect.size: opex creep failure band cited around $50k to $300k a month in revenue-adjacent spend

risk.note: A budget gate before hiring or adding fixed cost.

prerequisites: Opex by line, fixed vs variable
Current LTGP:CAC
steps: Track opex as a percent of revenue every month against 6 months ago.
Before adding any fixed cost, confirm the current LTGP:CAC can carry it.
Cut fixed cost sized for a past revenue peak (for example, hiring from a prior demand spike) rather than the current run rate.
Remember marketing spend, not headcount or office cost, is usually the main growth lever, so protect that line differently.

test.method: Review opex % of revenue and LTGP:CAC together monthly.
test.read_point: Monthly, and before any hire or fixed-cost commitment

title: Question any headline growth number before repeating it
hypothesis: If we ask what month an ARR was annualized from, what is funding a cash-flow-positive claim, and whether any cohort has reached a stated LTV horizon, then we do not build a plan on a headline number that does not hold up.

signal.check: A growth number (ARR, cash-flow positive, a stated LTV:CAC) is being used in planning without checking its basis.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a due-diligence habit, not a metric lift

risk.note: A questioning habit; applies to the brand's own claims as much as a competitor's.

steps: Ask what month an ARR figure was annualized from and compare it to a rolling 3 to 6 month average.
Ask what is funding any 'cash-flow positive' claim (financing, factoring, a facility).
Ask whether any cohort has actually reached the stated LTV horizon or if it is modelled.
Apply the same questions to the brand's own numbers before they are quoted externally.

test.method: Run this audit before any external claim or internal plan is finalized.
test.measure: whether each headline number's basis was checked
test.read_point: Before quoting or planning against any headline growth figure

title: Set the executive dashboard to profit contribution, AMER and CAC, not ROAS
hypothesis: If the executive dashboard leads with new-customer profit contribution, AMER and CAC instead of blended ROAS, then decisions stop chasing a metric that skews toward existing customers and branded search.

signal.check: The team's main dashboard leads with blended ROAS or email-attributed revenue as the headline number.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reporting discipline change, aiming for the lowest ROAS that is still profitable rather than the highest ROAS

risk.note: A dashboard change.

prerequisites: New vs returning revenue split
AMER computed
steps: Set the dashboard order: new-customer profit contribution, then AMER and new-customer revenue and orders, then CAC.
Move blended ROAS and email-attributed revenue to a supporting view, not the headline.
Aim for the lowest ROAS the brand can acquire profitably at, not the highest.
Treat a healthy ROAS next to flat topline as a sign that new and existing spend are not separated.

test.method: Compare decisions made under the old vs new dashboard for one quarter.
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Match the measurement tier to the size of the decision being made
hypothesis: If small daily calls use platform metrics, budget calls use finance-grade metrics like AMER and CAC, and large strategy calls use causal lift tests, then measurement effort scales with the size of the decision instead of adding tools that compound confusion.

signal.check: The brand has added dashboards, tools or conversion events recently without a clear tier they serve.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: A process change to the measurement stack.

steps: Map current tools and metrics to the reliability ladder: opinion, platform ROAS, marketing mix models, quasi-experiments, geo holdouts.
Match the tier to decision size: platform metrics for daily calls, AMER and profit contribution for budget calls, causal lift for large strategy calls.
Subtract tools and events that do not map to a real decision instead of adding more.
Reserve incrementality testing mainly for larger-scale decisions where the spend justifies it.

test.method: Audit the measurement stack against this tier map.
test.measure: count of tools mapped to a real decision
test.read_point: Once, then at each stage review

title: Require 2 or more consecutive weak quarters before reacting to a slow period as a crisis
hypothesis: If we require 2 or more consecutive weak quarters, not one, before treating a slow period as a strategy failure, then the brand avoids panic decisions during a normal plateau that many real brands went through before scaling.

signal.check: A single slow month or quarter has triggered a major strategy reset without checking for a 2-quarter pattern.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a patience rule, not a growth lift

risk.note: A decision-timing rule.

steps: Before a major reset, check whether the slowdown has lasted 2 or more consecutive quarters, not one.
Separate a genuine plateau from a data-integrity or seasonal artifact first (section A1 check).
If it is a true multi-quarter plateau, run the bottleneck diagnosis before changing strategy.

test.method: Track quarterly revenue and unit economics trend before any reset decision.
test.read_point: At each quarterly review

title: Add marketplace and payment commission as its own true gross margin line
hypothesis: If we add marketplace and payment-processor commission as its own cost line next to shipping and pick and pack, then true gross margin does not overstate profit on marketplace or processor-heavy sales.
does_not_apply_when: A pure DTC store with standard card processing fees already tagged

signal.check: True gross margin is computed without a separate line for marketplace or non-standard payment commission.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a rate, verify against the brand's actual marketplace or processor contract

risk.note: A cost-model addition.

prerequisites: Marketplace or processor fee schedule
steps: Pull the actual commission or fee rate from each marketplace or processor contract.
Add it as its own line in the true gross margin build, next to shipping and pick and pack.
Recompute true gross margin for marketplace-sold SKUs separately from DTC-sold ones.

test.method: Compare true gross margin with and without the commission line.
test.read_point: Once, then whenever a marketplace fee schedule changes

title: Track reverse logistics cost as its own line, not folded into a refund-rate haircut
hypothesis: If we track return shipping, restocking and inspection cost as its own line, then true gross margin reflects the real cost of a high-return category instead of only a revenue haircut.
does_not_apply_when: A category with a genuinely low return rate where the cost is immaterial

signal.check: Refund rate is subtracted from revenue but no separate processing-cost figure exists for returns.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a per-return cost, verify against 3PL or in-house handling cost

risk.note: A cost-model addition.

prerequisites: 3PL or in-house cost data for return handling
steps: Get the actual per-return cost of return shipping, restocking and inspection from the 3PL or ops team.
Add it as its own line in the cost-of-delivery build.
Recompute true gross margin for any SKU with a non-trivial return rate.

test.method: Compare true gross margin with and without the reverse logistics line.
test.read_point: Once, then whenever return volume changes materially

title: Add customer service cost per order to the unit-economics and cash model
hypothesis: If we add a customer service cost per order or per ticket to the unit-economics model, then the cash model reflects the real cost of support instead of treating it as free.

signal.check: The cash model has no line for customer service or support cost per order.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a cost-per-order figure, verify against the brand's own support headcount and ticket volume

risk.note: A cost-model addition.

prerequisites: Support headcount cost and ticket or order volume
steps: Divide monthly support cost by order volume or ticket count to get a per-order or per-ticket figure.
Add it to the 6-lever cash model alongside CAC, AOV, markup, returning rate, sell-through and opex.
Track it over time as order volume changes.

test.method: Recompute the per-order support cost quarterly.
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Split MER and AMER separately for marketplace revenue on a mixed-channel store
hypothesis: If we compute MER and AMER separately for marketplace revenue, then paid media performance is not distorted by marketplace orders that are not driven by the brand's own paid spend.
does_not_apply_when: A store with marketplace revenue under about 10% of total, where the distortion is small

signal.check: MER or AMER is computed on blended revenue that includes a meaningful marketplace share.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source addresses this split directly, verify against the brand's own marketplace revenue share

risk.note: A reporting split.

prerequisites: Revenue tagged by channel including marketplace
steps: Separate marketplace revenue from DTC revenue before computing MER and AMER.
Compute MER and AMER on DTC revenue only for paid-media accountability.
Report marketplace revenue and its own economics (commission, ad spend if any) separately.

test.method: Compare blended vs split MER/AMER for one quarter.
test.measure: amer gap between blended and DTC-only
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Fix the one binding growth constraint before touching the other two
hypothesis: If we name the one binding constraint (traffic, funnel or backend) and work only that, then effort does not get spread across every lever at once, which makes it impossible to tell what worked.
does_not_apply_when: A deliberate 2 to 3 lever cash move with a kept baseline, which is a planned exception, not working everything at once

signal.check: More than one major lever (creative, offer, page, channel) is being changed at the same time with no plan to isolate which one worked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline, not a metric target

risk.note: A sequencing decision.

prerequisites: Bottleneck diagnosis output naming the constraint
steps: Name the one binding constraint from the 3-layer read.
Work only that lever until it moves or is ruled out.
Hold other levers steady during the test window.
Move to the next constraint only after this one is resolved or confirmed not binding.

test.method: Track the targeted metric while holding other levers constant.
test.read_point: After the agreed test window for that lever

title: Run the 9-point data integrity checklist before any bottleneck diagnosis
hypothesis: If we check for 1-day view attribution, existing customers in cold campaigns, missing COGS tags, and 6 other integrity gaps before diagnosing a slowdown, then we do not chase a strategy problem that is really a measurement problem.

signal.check: Profitability has degraded and the team is discussing traffic, creative or seasonality without first ruling out a measurement issue.

expected_effect.size: one source estimates data integrity explains about 30% of audits, not the 80% its own title claims; carry 30%

risk.note: A checklist run.

prerequisites: Access to attribution settings and campaign structure
steps: Check for 1-day view still driving headline ROAS.
Check existing customers are excluded from cold campaigns.
Check COGS is tagged and new vs returning revenue is split.
Check any traffic, reach or DPA campaign has a real measurement plan.
Check for over-segmentation and fake-high tertiary-channel ROAS.
Fix what is broken, then re-read the month's numbers before diagnosing further.

test.method: Run the checklist before every bottleneck diagnosis.
test.read_point: At the start of every bottleneck diagnosis

title: Read the CAC and LTGP series before defaulting to traffic, creative or seasonality
hypothesis: If we read CAC and LTGP month over month before blaming traffic, creative or seasonality, then we catch a death spiral early instead of trying a new platform or agency on a bad ratio.

signal.check: Profitability is degrading and the first response under discussion is a new platform, agency or creative push rather than a CAC and LTGP read.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnosis-order rule

risk.note: A diagnosis-order rule.

prerequisites: Monthly CAC and LTGP series
steps: Pull CAC month over month with new-customer volume and revenue.
Check whether CAC is breaking upward while volume falls and spend was raised to hold revenue.
If so, treat it as a possible death spiral before trying a new platform, agency or creative push.
Only move to traffic, creative or seasonality explanations once this is ruled out.

test.method: Review the CAC/LTGP series before any major channel or agency change.
test.read_point: Before any new platform, agency or creative-strategy change

title: Run the 3-layer read: ads, funnel, backend, before picking a lever
hypothesis: If we instrument and read the ads layer (CPM, CPC, CTR, hook rate), the funnel layer (conversion rate times AOV) and the backend layer (repeat rate, LTV) together, then the actual weak layer is found instead of guessed from one metric.

signal.check: A performance problem is being diagnosed from one metric (like ROAS) without checking all 3 layers.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a diagnostic method

risk.note: A read-only diagnostic pass.

prerequisites: Funnel step data: ad, landing view, add to cart, checkout, purchase
steps: Instrument every funnel step: ad, landing page view, add to cart, checkout, purchase.
Read the ads layer against the brand's own historical CPM, CPC, CTR and hook rate.
Read the funnel layer as conversion rate times AOV against the brand's own baseline.
Read the backend layer as repeat rate and LTV.
Name the layer with the biggest gap from baseline as the likely constraint, not just the weakest absolute number.

test.method: Run the 3-layer read whenever performance drops.
test.measure: which layer shows the largest gap from baseline
test.read_point: At the start of every bottleneck diagnosis

title: Use the 2-signal read to tell a creative, funnel or price problem apart
hypothesis: If the platform will not spend, it is a creative or hook problem; if it spends but does not return money, it is a funnel or offer problem; if clicks are cheap but carts are abandoned, it is a price or offer problem, not the ad.

signal.check: An ad account is underperforming and the team has not separated whether spend is being delivered, converted, or held at checkout.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a triage method

risk.note: A read-only triage step.

prerequisites: Baseline CPM and CPC for the niche
steps: Check if the platform is delivering spend at a reasonable CPM for the niche; if not, treat it as a creative or hook problem.
If it spends but returns little revenue, check the landing page, offer and checkout.
If clicks are cheap and qualified but carts are abandoned, treat it as a price or offer problem, not a creative one.
Before rebuilding a page, test 4 to 5 angles against the current page for 1 to 2 days to see if messaging, not the page, is the gap.

test.method: Run this triage before deciding what to fix.
test.read_point: At the start of any underperformance investigation

title: Screen paid-traffic scalability with conversion rate times AOV against your own CPC
hypothesis: If conversion rate percent times AOV is well under about 300 relative to a roughly $3 CPC, then fixing conversion rate or AOV comes before adding more spend.
does_not_apply_when: A brand whose own CPC and margin differ a lot from the $3 reference; recompute the threshold from its own numbers

signal.check: Spend is being added while conversion rate times AOV sits well below the brand's own recomputed scalability threshold.

expected_effect.size: reference: 3% x $100 = 300; 5% x $60 and 1% x $300 also qualify

risk.note: A screening calculation.

prerequisites: Conversion rate, AOV and CPC history
steps: Compute conversion rate percent times AOV.
Recompute the 300-equivalent threshold from the brand's own CPC and margin, not the generic $3 CPC reference.
If well under the threshold, fix conversion rate or AOV, whichever is cheaper to move, before adding spend.
Re-run micro-CRO wins only after this screen passes.

test.method: Recompute the screen monthly against current CPC.
test.read_point: Before any spend increase

title: Name the brand's growth archetype before picking a lever
hypothesis: If we classify the brand as product-led, media-led or harvest-only before choosing a lever, then the fix matches the actual growth engine instead of copying a lever from the wrong archetype.

signal.check: A growth lever is being chosen without first naming whether the brand is product-led, media-led or harvest-only.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a classification step

risk.note: A read-only classification.

prerequisites: Reorder data, creative volume history, ad-set awareness-stage tags
steps: Check product-led signs: reorders with average ads, unprompted customer content, sales without paid support.
Check media-led signs: growth tracking creative volume and spend.
Check harvest-only signs: most ads in the bottom 2 awareness stages, celebrity names carrying prospecting, no cold-prospecting creative that would survive alone.
Pick the lever that matches: fix the offer or launch for product-led, add creative volume for media-led, build problem-first creative for harvest-only.

test.method: Re-run the archetype read whenever the growth lever is being chosen.
test.read_point: At the start of any lever decision

title: Run real spend across several personas and angles before calling it a product problem
hypothesis: If we run real ads, UGC, email and site work across several personas and angles for a meaningful window and check price against the target, then a true product-market-fit failure is not confused with a messaging or pricing problem.

signal.check: The team is ready to call a launch a product failure without having tested multiple personas, angles and a price change.

expected_effect.size: one repriced launch went from $10k against a $100k target to $150k in 2 weeks after a price cut

risk.note: Requires real ad spend and creative production before concluding anything.

prerequisites: Enough runway for a meaningful test window across personas
steps: Run ads, UGC content, email flows and site work across several personas and angles.
Test a price change before blaming the product; check price against the target customer's willingness to pay.
If friction persists across every demographic, angle and price tested, treat it as a real product-market-fit issue.
If it persists only at one price or with one angle, treat it as a pricing or messaging problem instead.

test.method: Run the multi-persona, multi-angle, price-inclusive test for a defined window.
test.measure: cvr_overall and revenue by persona/angle/price combination
test.read_point: After the agreed test window (illustrative horizon in the source is around 2 years for a full read, but a partial read at 8 to 12 weeks can rule out the easy fixes first)

title: Check creative volume against spend before blaming optimization
hypothesis: If we check new creative volume per month against the brand's own historical spend-per-creative-unit ratio, then a stalled account is diagnosed as a creative supply problem instead of a targeting or bid problem.

signal.check: Spend has stalled or frequency is climbing and new creative volume has not been checked against the brand's own spend-per-creative history.

expected_effect.size: reference points cited: roughly 1 new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend, or one creative unit sustaining about $2,500 of spend, varies widely by account

risk.note: A production-planning check.

prerequisites: Historical creative count and spend by month
steps: Compute the brand's own historical ratio of spend per active creative unit.
Compare current new-creative volume per month to what that ratio implies is needed.
If volume is below the brand's own ratio, treat it as a supply gap before touching bids or targeting.
Only count creative above a minimum quality bar; more low-quality ads does not fix the ceiling.

test.method: Track new creative volume against spend monthly.
test.measure: creatives launched vs the ratio implied by spend
test.read_point: Monthly

title: Diagnose a stalled angle as a TAM ceiling and open a new persona, not a bid fix
hypothesis: If frequency climbs and spend stalls on one angle, then the fix is a new persona or angle, not a bigger bid, because each angle has a finite audience that actually has that problem.

signal.check: One angle's frequency is climbing while its spend absorption flattens or falls.

expected_effect.size: no numeric ceiling given; needs the brand's own frequency and spend-by-angle history

risk.note: A diagnosis step before a creative decision.

prerequisites: Frequency and spend history by angle
steps: Track frequency and spend by angle over time.
When frequency climbs and spend absorption flattens on one angle, treat it as a TAM ceiling for that angle.
Open a new persona or angle rather than raising bids on the saturated one.
Note that stacking multiple angle TAMs is what lets one SKU absorb more total spend.

test.method: Track frequency and spend by angle monthly.
test.read_point: Monthly, or whenever an angle's spend stalls

title: Run root-cause diagnosis top-down: business, channel, campaign type, campaign, submetric
hypothesis: If we diagnose a performance drop top-down (business, then channel weighted by spend share, then campaign type, then campaign, then submetric) with a written discipline sentence, then the fix targets the real driver instead of the first metric noticed.

signal.check: A performance drop is being explained without a completed 'underperforming because X dropped, driven by Y, caused by Z' sentence.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline method

risk.note: A read-only diagnostic method.

prerequisites: Revenue = sessions x conversion rate x AOV decomposition by channel
steps: Check the dominant channel by spend share first.
Decompose revenue = sessions x conversion rate x AOV and identify which factor moved.
Extend the time window to avoid small-sample bias; use conversions by conversion time to avoid a false recent-days dip.
Write the discipline sentence: 'underperforming because [metric] dropped, driven by [submetric], caused by [trigger]'.
Make a targeted fix to the specific thing named, not a full rebuild, unless it is an emergency.

test.method: Require the discipline sentence before any change is approved.
test.measure: whether the sentence can be completed with real data
test.read_point: Before any performance-driven change

title: Check outside-account events before crediting an inside-account tweak
hypothesis: If we list influencer deals, retail openings, PR and channel launches in the window before crediting a recovery to a bid or budget tweak, then we do not over-credit an inside change for a swing that outside events actually caused.

signal.check: A recovery or improvement is being credited to an ad-account change without checking for outside events in the same window.

expected_effect.size: at very large scale, an inside-account tweak adds about 1% to a campaign; outside levers move far more

risk.note: A checking step before a claim is made.

prerequisites: A calendar of influencer, retail, PR and channel-launch events
steps: List influencer deals, retail openings, PR moments and channel launches in the window being reviewed.
Size the plausible inside-account effect against the size of the swing.
If the swing is much larger than what an inside tweak could plausibly cause, credit the outside event instead.
Never credit a channel launched into a seasonal peak with the peak's own lift without a causal design.

test.method: Cross-check every claimed recovery against the outside-event calendar.
test.measure: whether an outside event explains more of the swing than the inside change
test.read_point: Whenever a recovery or lift is being reported

title: Judge acquisition health on a weekly window, not a single day
hypothesis: If we judge acquisition health weekly or monthly instead of daily, then a single retention email send cannot flip the read on blended ROAS and cause a panic reaction.
does_not_apply_when: A brand-new store still validating demand, which may need daily monitoring

signal.check: A same-day swing in blended ROAS, often around an email send, triggered an ad-account change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a judging-cadence rule

risk.note: A cadence rule.

steps: Commit to a weekly or monthly read of acquisition unit economics before any deliberate spend-mix change.
Do not react to a single day's blended ROAS, especially around a retention send.
Treat intraday panic reactions as a pattern to watch for and stop.

test.method: Compare decisions made on a daily read vs a weekly read for one quarter.
test.read_point: Quarterly review

title: Treat intuition as accumulated test history, not a launch signal for an early brand
hypothesis: If we compare a strong feeling against the brand's own test history and runway before acting on it, then intuition is used where it has been earned and data is used where it has not.
does_not_apply_when: A mature, well-capitalized, second-time founder with a proven test history, for whom intuition carries more weight

signal.check: A launch or spend decision is being made on a strong feeling with no comparison to the brand's own test history.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a calibration rule

risk.note: A decision-check habit.

prerequisites: A record of the brand's own past test results
steps: Before acting on a strong feeling, check it against the brand's own test history and runway.
For an early or resource-constrained brand, treat the feeling as a hypothesis to test cheaply, not a launch signal.
For a brand with deep test history, give intuition more weight, but still record the call.

test.method: Log intuition-based calls and their outcomes over time.
test.measure: hit rate of intuition-based calls vs tested calls
test.read_point: Reviewed quarterly

title: Validate demand in cheap stages before any paid spend at launch
hypothesis: If a new store validates demand through a sales-threshold email test, then an organic post volume test, then a small fixed paid test in that order, then it avoids stacking an unproven product on unproven creative and unproven media buying at once.

signal.check: A new store is about to run paid ads without first testing demand through email or organic posts.

expected_effect.size: one reference: about $300 validates a low-priced product, about $2,000 takes a store from nothing to validated

risk.note: A staged, low-spend validation approach.

prerequisites: A product ready to sell
A small list or organic posting ability
steps: Email the product design or offer to any existing list with a sales threshold to hit before proceeding.
Post about 50 organic short-form pieces and watch for an outlier performance above baseline.
Run a small fixed paid test ($10 to 50 a day) with 1 to 3 new creatives every few days, reading on 2 signals: does it spend, does it convert.
Only scale paid spend after the cheaper stages show a real signal.

test.method: Run the 3 stages in order and record the outcome of each.
test.measure: signal strength at each stage (email response, organic outlier, paid 2-signal read)
test.read_point: About 2 weeks for the paid stage at $10 a day

title: Stand up welcome and abandoned-cart flows before scaling paid at launch
hypothesis: If welcome and abandoned-cart flows are live before paid spend is scaled, then the store captures revenue from the traffic it already earned instead of leaking it while all attention goes to paid.

signal.check: Paid spend is being scaled and no welcome or abandoned-cart flow exists yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a launch-order rule, not a stated lift here

risk.note: A one-time setup task.

prerequisites: Email/SMS platform connected to the store
steps: Build a welcome flow for new subscribers.
Build an abandoned-cart flow.
Confirm both are live and tested before increasing paid budget.
Do not aim for a perfect subscription or margin setup at the expense of getting these live.

test.method: Check flow revenue share once flows are live.
test.read_point: 30 days after flows go live

title: Build the growth model sheet and start a monthly CAC/LTGP table at $100k to $1M
hypothesis: If a store builds the P&L waterfall, true gross margin per SKU and a monthly CAC/LTGP table once it passes about $100k revenue, then unit economics are known before volume is added, not discovered after.

signal.check: The store has passed roughly $100k in revenue without a P&L waterfall, true gross margin per SKU, or a monthly CAC/LTGP table.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a stage-appropriate build, not a stated lift

risk.note: A reporting build.

prerequisites: 12 months of order data
Per-SKU cost data
steps: Build the P&L waterfall and true gross margin per SKU.
Start a monthly CAC and LTGP:CAC table.
Tag COGS per SKU.
Set up 7-day-click Meta reporting with existing customers excluded from cold campaigns.
Build a daily dashboard of new-customer profit contribution, revenue, orders and blended CAC.

test.method: Confirm all pieces are in place at the stage review.
test.measure: presence of each measurement item vs the $100k to $1M checklist
test.read_point: Quarterly stage review

title: Hire finance capability and watch opex creep in the $100k to $1M stage
lever: early finance hire and opex watch
hypothesis: If a store hires a strong finance capability or fractional CFO early in this stage rather than a year before a sale, then opex creep is caught in the $50k to $300k a month band where it most often kills brands.

signal.check: The store is past $100k revenue with no finance capability and no regular opex-vs-revenue check.

expected_effect.size: opex creep failure band cited around $50k to $300k a month

risk.note: A hiring and monitoring decision.

steps: Hire a fractional CFO or strong finance owner at this stage, not the year before a sale.
Set a monthly opex-vs-revenue check.
Flag any fixed cost added without a matching LTGP:CAC check.
Watch for opex creep specifically in the $50k to $300k a month spend band.

test.method: Review opex percent of revenue monthly.
test.read_point: Monthly, starting the month the finance hire begins

title: Add in-platform lift tests and incremental attribution once spend passes $100k a month
hypothesis: If a store adds in-platform lift tests and incremental attribution once monthly spend or revenue passes the $5 to 20M band, then attribution does not silently break as the account gets more complex.
does_not_apply_when: A store still under about $1M revenue, where 7-day click and COGS tagging is the right measurement tier

signal.check: Monthly spend or revenue is well past the early-stage band and no lift test or incremental attribution layer exists yet.

expected_effect.size: attribution is described as starting to break above about $100k a month of spend

risk.note: A measurement-tooling addition.

prerequisites: 7-day click and COGS tagging already in place
steps: Confirm 7-day click and COGS tagging are already solid.
Add in-platform lift tests as a second validation layer.
Move toward geo-lift and an omnichannel dashboard as the store approaches $20M+.
Apply incrementality factors to platform ROAS before reallocating budget.

test.method: Compare platform-attributed ROAS to lift-test results.
test.measure: gap between attributed and incremental read
test.read_point: After the first lift test completes

title: Hire in order: founder's weakest function, then a paid-media owner, then a CMO
hypothesis: If hiring follows the order of the founder's weakest function, then a dedicated paid-media owner, then a CMO, then the founder stops being the bottleneck at the point where it matters most instead of hiring a CMO too early.

signal.check: The founder is still running the weakest function personally past the $1M to $10M stage, or a CMO was hired before a paid-media owner.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a hiring-sequence rule from founder self-reports

risk.note: Hiring the wrong role first can waste months of runway and a salary.

prerequisites: A clear task audit of what the founder still does personally
steps: Audit which function the founder is weakest at or spends the most low-value time on.
Hire an ops generalist or specialist for that function first.
Hire a dedicated paid-media owner next.
Hire a CMO only after that, once there is a media function to manage.
Keep the decision loop at 5 to 8 people or fewer.

test.method: Track founder hours on the weakest function before and after each hire.
test.measure: founder hours spent on the delegated function
test.read_point: 3 months after each hire

title: Sequence acquisition first, then a dedicated retention phase starting with the offer
hypothesis: If a store proves acquisition first and then runs a dedicated retention phase starting with the offer and subscription structure rather than small loyalty assets, then retention effort goes to the biggest lever first.
does_not_apply_when: A consumable category, where cheap flows and a subscription option should exist from day one regardless of sequencing

signal.check: Acquisition is proven but no deliberate retention phase has started, or the first retention effort was a small loyalty asset instead of the offer structure.

expected_effect.size: one example spent its first 9 to 12 months on acquisition only, then made a prepaid tier its first retention move

risk.note: A sequencing decision.

prerequisites: Acquisition proven with stable CAC and LTGP:CAC
steps: Confirm acquisition is proven with stable CAC and LTGP:CAC before adding a dedicated retention phase.
Start the retention phase with the offer and subscription structure, not a loyalty page or points program.
Check the category repeat band before setting retention expectations.
Add smaller loyalty assets only after the offer-level retention work is live.

test.method: Track repeat_rate_90d before and after the retention phase starts.
test.read_point: One quarter after the retention phase launches

title: Set a sustainable pace and size support and inventory before pushing to the next revenue tier
hypothesis: If a store sets an internal sustainable-pace target and sizes support and inventory for the spike before pushing to the next tier, then a promotion-driven sellout does not force an ad-account reset and a support crisis.

signal.check: A push to the next revenue tier is planned without a sized support and inventory plan for the resulting spike.

expected_effect.size: one example needed 3 months to restock and 40 extra support reps in a month after a sellout

risk.note: Underestimating the spike can force withholding sends and resetting the ad account's learning phase.

prerequisites: Inventory and support capacity data
steps: Set an internal sustainable-pace revenue target before pushing to the next tier.
Size inventory buffer and support headcount for the expected spike.
Confirm restock lead time and support hiring can keep pace before launching the push.
Plan to withhold marketing sends if inventory or support falls behind, rather than after the fact.

test.method: Compare actual vs planned support and stock levels during the push.
test.measure: stockout_days and ticket_backlog during the spike
test.read_point: During and immediately after the tier push

title: Manage currency and FX exposure as its own decision for multi-currency stores
hypothesis: If a store transacting or sourcing in more than one currency manages FX exposure as its own decision, then currency swings do not silently erode margin that looks fine in local-currency reporting.
does_not_apply_when: A store that transacts and sources in a single currency

signal.check: The store transacts or sources in more than one currency with no FX hedging or exposure review.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source covers hedging mechanics, verify against the brand's own FX exposure

risk.note: An unmanaged FX position can erase margin gains from other levers.

prerequisites: A list of currencies used in sourcing and sales
steps: List every currency used in sourcing costs and sales revenue.
Size the exposure (revenue or cost at risk from a currency move).
Decide on a hedging approach or accept the exposure deliberately, with finance sign-off.
Review the exposure at each stage review.

test.method: Review FX exposure quarterly.
test.read_point: Quarterly

title: Build channel mix from each channel's own frontier, not a fixed percent template
hypothesis: If we push each channel to the point where its incremental AMER hits break-even and move the next dollar to whichever channel is furthest from its frontier, then budget stops following a fixed percentage template that ignores each channel's real headroom.

signal.check: Channel budget is set by a fixed percent split rather than by each channel's incremental AMER versus break-even.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a reallocation method

risk.note: A reallocation plan; each move should carry a confirmation window.

prerequisites: Per-channel incremental read or an experienced buyer's judgment where no lift test exists
steps: Estimate each channel's incremental AMER, from a lift test where available or an experienced judgment otherwise.
Find the point where each channel's incremental AMER would hit break-even.
Move the next dollar to the channel furthest below its own frontier.
Reallocate gradually and confirm the read weekly for at least 4 weeks.

test.method: Track incremental AMER by channel after each reallocation.
test.read_point: Weekly for 4 weeks after each reallocation

title: Treat a very high ROAS on a tiny tertiary-channel spend as a red flag, not a win
hypothesis: If a very high ROAS shows up on a low-spend tertiary channel, then treat it as likely warm-only delivery and confirm with a lift read before crediting or scaling it.

signal.check: A tertiary channel (Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit, Pinterest, X) shows an unusually high ROAS at very low spend with no lift test done.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a validation step, not a lift itself

risk.note: A validation check before scaling.

steps: Flag any tertiary channel with a ROAS far above the account average at low spend.
Run a lift read (holdout or geo test) before crediting the channel or scaling it.
Only scale the channel once the lift read confirms incremental value.

test.method: Run a holdout or geo-lift test on the flagged channel.
test.read_point: After the lift test completes, typically 2 to 4 weeks

title: Scale the primary channel to its named headroom before adding a new channel
hypothesis: If we name the primary channel's remaining headroom and confirm creative capacity before adding a second channel, then a new channel is funded as a real experiment instead of a reallocation away from a channel that still has room.

signal.check: A new channel is being added or funded without a stated estimate of the primary channel's remaining headroom.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a sequencing rule

risk.note: A sequencing and funding decision.

prerequisites: Primary channel spend and incremental read history
steps: Estimate the primary channel's remaining headroom before its incremental AMER hits break-even.
Confirm creative production can feed a second channel without starving the first.
Fund the new channel as a separate experiment with its own creative and success criteria, not by reallocating from the core channel.
Do not credit or blame the new channel for a swing that overlaps with the primary channel; test for cannibalization first.

test.method: Track primary-channel headroom and new-channel results separately.
test.measure: primary channel incremental AMER; new channel's own success criteria
test.read_point: Before launch, then monthly

title: Route 80 to 90% of ecommerce Google spend to Shopping and verify PMax with a holdout
hypothesis: If most ecommerce Google spend goes to Shopping and PMax and branded search are verified with holdouts before scaling, then Google spend is not quietly captured by demand that would have converted anyway.

signal.check: PMax or branded search holds a large share of Google spend with no holdout test run on it.

expected_effect.size: PMax cited at 20 to 40% of Google spend for mid to upper ecommerce; branded search capped near 1% by one high-awareness brand's own holdouts

risk.note: A verification step before scaling Google spend.

prerequisites: Ability to run a Google holdout test
steps: Route the bulk of Google ecommerce spend to Shopping.
Run a holdout on branded search and on PMax to see how much revenue is truly incremental.
Cap or protect branded search based on the brand's own holdout result and awareness level, not a borrowed percentage.
Treat Google as a preparation platform, not a scaling platform, during a peak sale.

test.method: Run a Google branded-search and PMax holdout.
test.measure: incremental revenue from the holdout vs attributed revenue
test.read_point: After the holdout completes, typically 4 or more weeks

title: Start creator and affiliate deals broad and cheap, then narrow to a few deep commission partners
hypothesis: If we start broad and cheap with many creators, learn who moves product, then narrow to a few long-term deep partnerships on commission, then creator spend converges on the partners who actually sell instead of staying spread thin.

signal.check: The creator program has run for 3 or more months with no narrowing from a broad flat-fee pool to a commission-based core.

expected_effect.size: one example narrowed from 50 to 500 creators down to about 300 after learning who moved product

risk.note: A phased program; early cost is a learning cost.

prerequisites: Tracking (codes or links) to identify which creators convert
steps: Recruit a broad, cheap pool of creators to start (micro-creators, a floor payment or low commission).
Track which creators actually move product using codes or links.
Narrow to a smaller group of deep, long-term partners.
Move winning partners to commission-only once they have proven volume.

test.method: Track conversion and revenue per creator over the program.
test.read_point: After the initial broad phase, typically 8 to 12 weeks

title: Use codes and links plus a post-purchase survey instead of a zero-attribution creator program
hypothesis: If we default to codes, URLs and a post-purchase survey for creator attribution instead of judging on blended signals alone, then most stores can tell which creators actually drive sales.
does_not_apply_when: A brand where DTC is under about 5% of revenue and a huge creator bench makes code tracking impractical

signal.check: Creator or influencer spend is judged only on views, content volume and blended signals with no codes, links or survey data.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a tracking-method choice

risk.note: A tracking setup, not a live spend change.

prerequisites: A post-purchase survey tool
steps: Assign a unique code or URL to every creator or affiliate deal.
Add a post-purchase survey asking how the customer heard about the brand.
Compare survey-attributed share to spend share by creator.
Reserve a zero-attribution, blended-signal approach only for a DTC-light, omnichannel brand with a large creator bench.

test.method: Compare code-attributed and survey-attributed revenue by creator monthly.
test.read_point: Monthly

title: Prove one channel small and organic before scaling paid, when time is more available than money
hypothesis: If a founder with more time than budget builds an organic audience and creative proof point first, then paid spend later starts from creative and demand signals that are already proven, cutting wasted early ad spend.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with proven unit economics and creative capacity where demand is already known and paid can start immediately

signal.check: The team has budget pressure and no organic posting history, but is about to commit meaningful paid spend on unproven creative.

expected_effect.size: one example got about 70% of its best paid ads from organic winners

risk.note: Even a large organic following rarely reaches all its own followers, so this does not replace paid acquisition.

prerequisites: Ability to produce organic content regularly
steps: Post organic content regularly across the relevant platforms before scaling paid spend.
Track which organic pieces outperform baseline.
Turn outperforming organic content into paid creative.
Do not assume 'owning an audience' replaces paid acquisition; even a large following rarely reaches all of itself.

test.method: Compare paid performance of organic-derived creative vs cold-produced creative.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_overall by creative source
test.read_point: After the first paid test batch

title: Confirm channel overlap with a pause-one test before scaling either channel
hypothesis: If we pause one of two channels that may share demand and watch total revenue rather than the paused channel's own reported conversions, then we find out whether the two channels are cannibalizing each other before scaling either.

signal.check: Two channels serve an overlapping audience (for example Amazon and TikTok Shop, or Meta and branded search) and no pause-one or geo-holdout test has been run.

expected_effect.size: one example paused Amazon or TikTok Shop and saw no change in total revenue

risk.note: Pausing a channel temporarily for the test could dip revenue during the test window; keep the window short.

prerequisites: Ability to pause one channel without breaking fulfillment or reporting
steps: Identify a pair of channels that may share demand.
Pause one channel for a defined window.
Watch total revenue across both channels, not just the paused channel's own reported conversions.
Use the result to decide how to fund each channel going forward.

test.method: Run the pause-one test for 1 to 2 weeks.
test.measure: total revenue during the pause vs the prior comparable period
test.read_point: After the pause window ends

title: Coordinate paid spend with the owned calendar to avoid burning budget before a free conversion
hypothesis: If we pull paid spend back ahead of a known email drop, launch or discount push, then we do not pay for clicks that would have converted anyway once the owned send lands.

signal.check: Paid spend runs at full pace right before a planned email drop or discount push with no coordination.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a coordination rule

risk.note: A scheduling coordination.

prerequisites: A shared marketing calendar across paid and lifecycle teams
steps: Maintain a shared calendar of upcoming email drops, launches and discount pushes.
Pull paid spend back in the days just before a major owned-channel send.
Track daily discount rate and burn together so a rising discount rate with rising burn is caught.
Resume normal paid pacing once the owned push has run its course.

test.method: Compare paid efficiency around coordinated vs uncoordinated sends.
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 coordinated sends

title: Run each major new product category as its own acquisition business unit
hypothesis: If each major product category gets its own ad account, buyer and targets while email and storewide offers cross-sell across units, then a multi-category brand does not centralize acquisition under one buyer who cannot serve every customer type well.
does_not_apply_when: A single-hero-SKU brand with one clear customer type

signal.check: Multiple distinct product categories share one ad account, buyer and target set with no category-level ownership.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a structural rule from one multi-category operator

risk.note: A centralized CMO across brands with different customers is named as a failure pattern; avoid over-centralizing.

prerequisites: At least 2 distinct product categories with different customer bases
steps: Split ad accounts and targets by major product category.
Assign a buyer or owner per category business unit.
Keep email and storewide offers as the cross-sell layer across units.
Avoid centralizing all categories under one CMO with no category-level depth.

test.method: Compare cpa and cvr_overall per category before and after the split.
test.read_point: One quarter after the split

title: Plan for local payment methods and low-bandwidth PDPs before scaling into a mobile-first market
hypothesis: If we plan around local payment methods, cash on delivery where relevant and a low-bandwidth PDP before scaling spend into a mobile-first, non-US market, then checkout friction does not silently cap conversion in that market.
does_not_apply_when: A store not expanding into a mobile-first, non-Western-card market

signal.check: Spend is scaling into a mobile-first, non-US market without local payment methods or a page-weight check on the PDP.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a figure, verify against the target market's own payment mix

risk.note: Skipping local payment fit before scaling spend risks paying to acquire traffic that cannot check out.

prerequisites: Data on the target market's dominant payment methods and typical connection speed
steps: Check the target market's dominant payment methods, including cash on delivery where common.
Add the local payment methods to checkout before scaling spend there.
Test PDP load time on a low-bandwidth mobile connection representative of that market.
Fix any page-weight issue found before scaling paid spend into that market.

test.method: Compare cvr_checkout_to_order before and after local payment methods are added.
test.read_point: 4 weeks after the payment methods go live

title: Design a loyalty or membership program to its own ROI, not just as a warm-traffic landing page
hypothesis: If a loyalty or membership program is designed and measured on its own ROI rather than only used as a page to route warm traffic to, then the store knows whether the program itself pays for its cost, not just whether the page converts warm visitors.
does_not_apply_when: A store without enough repeat-purchase volume to support a program

signal.check: A loyalty or membership page exists and is routed warm traffic, but no one has measured its own cost against its own retained revenue.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source covers program design or ROI beyond routing, verify against the brand's own repeat data

risk.note: A measurement and design task.

prerequisites: Enough repeat-purchase volume to justify a program
steps: Estimate the program's cost (rewards, tech, admin).
Estimate the incremental repeat revenue it drives, using a holdout or before/after cohort comparison.
Route warm traffic to the page as a secondary tactic, not the program's justification.
Kill or redesign the program if its own ROI does not clear its cost.

test.method: Run a holdout of members vs a comparable non-member cohort.
test.read_point: 6 months after program launch

title: Give the real reason next to every small on-page ask
hypothesis: If every small on-page request (email capture, a size or fit question) shows its real reason, then the cue builds trust instead of becoming a manipulation risk if it were faked.

signal.check: A page asks for an email, a size, or other small detail with no stated reason.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism from a non-ecommerce study, apply as an honesty constraint not a guaranteed lift

risk.note: A copy change; never fake the reason given.

steps: List every small ask on the site (email capture, size question, fit quiz step).
Write the true reason for each ask next to it.
Remove or fix any ask whose real reason cannot be stated honestly.
Never use a fabricated reason to increase completion.

test.method: A/B test the page with and without the stated reason.
test.read_point: After enough sessions for a stable read, typically 2 to 4 weeks

title: Lead with a genuine gift or sample before asking for the order or email
hypothesis: If a real free sample, guide or gift-with-purchase comes before the ask, then reciprocity works honestly, unlike a discount dressed up as a gift.
does_not_apply_when: A discount presented as a gift, or a fictional premium tier used only as an anchor; both are banned forms

signal.check: A conversion-boosting offer is planned that asks for the order or email before giving anything real.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, no ecommerce-specific figure in this source

risk.note: The gift must be real and given before the ask, or reciprocity is not honestly earned.

prerequisites: A genuine sample, guide or gift to offer
steps: Create a real free sample, guide or gift with a genuine cost to the brand.
Give it before asking for the order or email, not after.
Never dress up a lowball discount as a free gift.
Track whether the gift-first sequence lifts conversion or email capture versus the ask-first version.

test.method: A/B test gift-first vs ask-first sequencing.
test.read_point: After enough sessions for a stable read

title: Set the welcome discount as a first-purchase incentive only, disclosed plainly for subscriptions
hypothesis: If the welcome discount is framed as a one-time first-purchase incentive with subscription terms disclosed plainly, then it converts the first order without training the customer to expect a permanent discount or hiding the real subscription cost.

signal.check: A welcome discount runs as a recurring reflex, or subscription terms and the post-discount price are not disclosed plainly at signup.

expected_effect.size: one source found a 10 to 20% welcome discount converted well with no added gain at 30%

risk.note: A copy and offer-structure change.

steps: Cap the welcome discount around 10 to 20% since deeper discounts showed no added gain.
Frame it explicitly as a first-purchase incentive, not an ongoing rate.
Disclose subscription terms and the post-discount price plainly at signup.
Check that the store's value proposition holds once the discount ends.

test.method: A/B test discount depth (10 vs 20 vs 30%) on first-purchase conversion.
test.read_point: After enough new-customer volume for a stable read

title: Show proof from a similar customer on ambiguous funnel steps, never a generic count
hypothesis: If proof on ambiguous funnel steps comes from a customer with the same body type or use case rather than a generic count, then social proof reads as credible instead of manufactured.
does_not_apply_when: A confident, high-intent buyer on a premium page, where heavy proof can read as desperate instead of helpful

signal.check: The funnel uses a generic 'X people bought this' or a static viewer count with no traceable order data behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mechanism-based, apply as an honesty constraint

risk.note: Every count shown must trace to a real order or platform number; fabricated counts are banned.

prerequisites: Real order or review data segmented by customer type or use case
